part_title: Sampling Controls, Token Choice and Latency
review_basis: Visually inspected original numbered WebP slides 05–07 individually, including illustrative probability values, temperature/top-k/top-p comparisons and latency pipeline; narration follows those exact visuals.

scenes.title: Token probabilities and sampling
scenes.narration: A language model generates text one token at a time. A token might be a whole word or just part of one. The first chart gives an invented example for 'After the rain, the streets were.' The next-token choices have probabilities: wet, zero point four; flooded, zero point two five; slippery, zero point one five; and empty and muddy, zero point one each. Notice the values add to one. The second panel shows sampling selecting 'wet.' A probability of forty percent does not mean the model must choose it every time; it is one candidate among several. Now look at the two street photographs below. After rain, 'wet' looks plausible. After a parade, the displayed distribution changes and 'empty' becomes the most likely example. The context before a token shapes its probability. On the bottom right, temperature illustrates another influence. Lower temperature favors higher-probability choices more strongly, while higher temperature allows more varied choices. The illustrated values are not real measurements. Sampling settings adjust how candidate tokens are chosen; they do not establish whether the statement is factually true. This is why a confident-sounding or frequently selected next word can still be wrong.

scenes.title: Optimize prompt performance
scenes.narration: This slide shows three controls that influence generation. First, the left panel introduces system instructions: the overall role, goals, rules and tone that guide the model's behavior. For example, a support assistant could be told to answer politely and use concise explanations. The center panel compares temperatures. Lower temperature concentrates selection on more likely tokens, often giving focused and consistent wording. Higher temperature allows a wider variety of ideas, which may help brainstorming but can also produce less predictable output. Now read the right panel. Top-k equals five restricts selection to the five most likely token candidates. Top-p equals zero point eight instead considers the smallest high-probability set whose cumulative probability reaches that threshold. The number of candidates can change from one step to another. These techniques may be combined where the selected model supports them. The bottom comparison suggests focused settings for structured tasks and more diversity for exploring ideas. But there is no universal temperature range of zero to one, and low values do not guarantee identical or correct answers. Change one setting at a time, compare actual results against your task requirements, and check the supported parameter ranges for the model you are using.

scenes.title: Understand prompt latency
scenes.narration: Latency is the time a user waits for an AI response. Follow the top pipeline. Your application sends a request, optional document retrieval or tool calls may run, Amazon Bedrock processes the prompt, and generated tokens stream back to the application. The lower left separates two measurements. Time to first token is how long it takes until the first piece of output arrives. Total response time is the wait until the final token has arrived. Streaming can make an application feel responsive even when the full answer still takes longer. Now check the factors panel: model choice and service load influence processing time, longer input prompts may take more work to process, and longer outputs usually require more generation time. Retrieval and tool calls also add steps before or during generation. The last panel shows temperature, top-p and top-k. They primarily affect token selection and are not guaranteed latency-reduction switches. Imagine a help desk assistant searching several policy documents before replying. A delay might come from retrieval rather than the model itself. Measure each stage before optimizing. If the main problem is total response time, shortening unnecessary output may help; if the first token is slow, investigate input processing, model load and upstream operations.
